lamblike.x: also lamb-like, "like a lamb, gentle, meek," early 15c., lombliche, from lamb (n.) + like (adj.). Chaucer has lambish "gentle."

lameness.x: "state of being lame, defect or unsoundness of a limb or limbs," 1520s, from lame (adj.) + -ness.

landfall.x:
1620s, "sighting of land," from land (n.) + fall (v.) in the sense of "happen." A word from the days of imprecise nautical navigation.
Land-fall. The first land discovered after a sea voyage. Thus a good land fall implies the land expected or desired; a bad landfall the reverse. [John Hamilton Moore, "The New Practical Navigator," London, 1814]
Also "an approaching or coming to land on a sea voyage" (by 1883). In reference to hurricanes, in the second sense, by 1932. Also occasionally "a landslide."

landlady.x: "woman who owns a house or land occupied by tenants," also "a landlord's wife," 1520s, from land (n.) + lady.

landless.x: "destitute of land, having no property in land," Middle English landlese, from Old English landleas; see land (n.) + -less. Compare Middle Low German lantlos. Related: Landlessness.

landline.x: also land-line, by 1861, originally in reference to a telegraph wire run over land (as opposed to under sea); from land (n.) + line (n.). It is attested by 1965 in reference to a telephone line which uses wire or some other material (distinguished from a radio or cellular line).

landmine.x: also land-mine, "explosive device placed on the ground (or just under it) as a weapon," 1871, from land (n.) + mine (n.2), which earlier had referred to sea weapons.

landward.x: "lying toward the land or away from the sea-coast," early 15c., from land (n.) + -ward. Compare Dutch landwaarts, Middle Low German landwert, German landwärts. As an adjective, "lying toward the land; interior, away from the coast," it is attested from 1530s.

larboard.x:
"left-hand side of a ship" (to a person on board and facing the bow), 1580s, alteration of Middle English ladde-borde (c. 1300), which is perhaps literally "the loading side," if this was the side on which goods were loaded onto a ship. In which case it would be from laden "to load" (see lade) + bord "ship's side" (see board (n.2)).
Altered 16c. by influence of starboard, then, to avoid confusion of similar-sounding words, it was largely replaced by the specialized sense of port (n.4). The Old English term for it was bæcbord, literally "back board" (compare starboard), a term which remains in the other Germanic tongues.

lateness.x: Middle English latnesse, from Old English lætness "slowness," from late (adj.) + -ness. It is attested from late 14c. as "a being advanced in time;" by 1877 as "a being behind the proper time" (as of a student for a class).

latesome.x: "somewhat late," Middle English latsom, from Old English lætsum "backward, slow, sluggish;" see late + -some (1). Related: Latesomeness. Also in the sense "somewhat late, slow, backward" (of fruit, etc.) was lateward (1530s).

latterly.x: "of late, lately, at a recent time," 1734, from latter (adj.) + -ly (2). Called by Johnson [1755] "a low word lately hatched." Related: Lattermost.

laudanum.x:
"tincture of opium," c. 1600, from Modern Latin laudanum (1540s), coined by Paracelsus for a medicine he mixed, supposed to contain gold and crushed pearls and many expensive ingredients, but probably owing its effectiveness to only one of them, opium.
Perhaps from Latin laudare "to praise" (see laud), or from Latin ladanum "a gum resin," from Greek ladanon, a word perhaps of Semitic origin. The word soon came to be used for "any alcoholic tincture of opium."
Latin ladanum had been used in Middle English from late 14c. in reference to plant resins, especially of certain shrubs in Iberia used in medicinal treatments, but this is not regarded as the immediate source of the 16c. word.

launcher.x: 1824, "one who launches" anything, agent noun from launch (v.). It is attested by 1911 as "device for launching," originally of airplanes; by 1944 in reference to rockets.

laureate.x:
"crowned with laurels" (as a mark of distinction), late 14c., earliest reference is to poetic distinction, from Latin laureatus "crowned with laurels," from laurea "laurel crown" (emblematic of victory or distinction in poetry), from fem. of laureus "of laurel," from laurus "laurel" (see laurel (n.)).
A poet laureate is one who has been publicly crowned with laurels by a sovereign or other eminent person in recognition of merits. Laureat poete is first found in Chaucer's "Canterbury Tales" (in reference to Petrarch — Fraunceys Petrak); it also was used in Middle English of Aesop and, by early 15c., of Chaucer himself. The first official one probably was Ben Jonson (1638), though the first recorded one was Dryden (1668). The inverted form poet laureate, in imitation of Latin word order, is attested in English from c. 1400.
As a noun, laureate is by 1520s, from the adjective or from a mistaken reading of poet laureate. Extended 1947 to Nobel prize winners. Related: Laureateship (1732), laureation.

lavalier.x: kind of ornament that hangs around the neck, 1873, from French lavallière, a kind of tie, after Louise Françoise de La Baume Le Blanc de La Vallière, Duchesse de La Vallière (1644-1710), mistress of Louis XIV from 1661-1667.

lawmaker.x: also law-maker, "legislator," late 15c., from law (n.) + maker.

laxative.x: late 14c., "causing relaxation or looseness," from Old French laxatif (13c.), from Medieval Latin laxativus "loosening," from Latin laxat-, past participle stem of laxare "loosen," from laxus "loose, lax" (see lax (adj.)). The noun meaning "a laxative medicine, a medicine that relieves constipation by relaxing the intestines" is from late 14c.

layabout.x: also lay-about, "habitual loafer," by 1930, from the verbal phrase; see lay (v.) + about (adv.). The notion is one who "lays about" public places, etc. The verbal phrase is attested by 1886 in reference to persons, "be prostrate and inert," with implications of indolence. Earlier it meant "lay siege to," and also "to strike on all sides," hence "act with vigor" (Middle English).

laywoman.x: 1520s, from lay (adj.) + woman; probably modeled on layman.

laziness.x: "aversion or indisposition to action or exertion," 1570s, from lazy + -ness.

leachate.x: "that which is formed by or results from leaching," 1920, from leach + -ate (1). The older noun was simply leach.

leathern.x: "of or like leather," Old English leðren, earlier liðerin; see leather + -en (2). Similar formation in Dutch lederen, Old High German lidirin, German ledern.

lecithin.x: fatty substance found in the yolks of eggs (among other places), 1853, from French lécithine (coined 1850 by French pharmacist Theodore N. Gobley), from Greek lekithos "egg yolk," + chemical suffix -ine (2). Greek lekithos is of unknown origin; Beekes writes that, "Because of the suffixes and the meaning, the word is clearly of Pre-Greek origin." Related: Lecithinase.

leftover.x: also left-over, "remaining, not used up," 1890, from left + over. The noun meaning "something left over" is from 1891; leftovers "excess food after a meal" (especially if re-served later) is from 1878; in this sense Old English had metelaf.

leftward.x: "to or toward the left or the left-hand side," late 15c., from left (adj.) + -ward. Related: Leftwards.

legalese.x: "the language of legal documents," 1914, from legal + language name ending -ese.

legalise.x: chiefly British English spelling of legalize; for suffix, see -ize. Related: Legalisation; legalised; legalising.

legality.x: mid-15c., "law-abiding behavior or character," from Medieval Latin legalitatem (nominative legalitas), from Latin legalis "pertaining to the law" (see legal).

legation.x: c. 1400, "mission of a deputy or envoy," from Old French legation "embassy, mission" and directly from Latin legationem (nominative legatio) "the office of an ambassador," noun of action from past participle stem of legare "send as a deputy" (see legate). From c. 1600 as "body of deputies sent, representatives," 1832 as "official residence of a diplomat."

let-down.x: also letdown, "a disappointment," 1768, from let (v.) + down (adv.). The verbal phrase is from mid-12c. in a literal sense "cause to be lowered," of drawbridges, etc.; figuratively by 1754.

leveller.x: also leveler, 1590s, someone or something that levels or makes even; agent noun from level (v.). In English history, from 1640s (with initial capital) as the name of a political party of the time of Charles I that advocated abolishing all differences of position and rank.

lie-down.x: period of rest reclining, 1840, from the verbal phrase (attested from c. 1200); see lie (v.2) + down (adv.).

lifelike.x: 1610s, "likely to live," from life (n.) + like (adj.). Meaning "exactly like the living original" is from 1725.

lifelong.x: also life-long, "continuing a lifetime," 1855, from life (n.) + long (adj.).

lifespan.x: also life-span, "length of time during which someone lives or something exists," 1918, from life (n.) + span (n.1). Often with a sense of "normal or average duration of life, life-expectancy."

liftable.x: "that may be lifted" in any sense of that word, 1833, from lift (v.) + -able.

likeable.x: also likable, 1730, a hybrid from like (v.) + -able. Related: Likeableness. Middle English had likeworthy (from Old English licwyrðe "agreeable, acceptable").

limerick.x:
type of nonsense verse of five lines, 1896, perhaps from the county and city of Limerick in Ireland, but if so the connection is obscure. Often (after OED's Murray) attributed to a party game in which each guest in turn made up a nonsense verse and all sang a refrain with the line "Will you come up to Limerick?" but he reported this in 1898 and earlier evidence is wanting. Or perhaps from Learic, from Edward Lear (1812-1888) English humorist who popularized the form. Earliest examples are in French, which further complicates the quest for the origin. OED's first record of the word is in a letter of Aubrey Beardsley.
 The limerick may be the only traditional form in English not borrowed from the poetry of another language. ... John Ciardi suggests that the Irish Brigade, which served in France for most of the eighteenth century, might have taken the form to France or developed an English version of a French form. ... The contemporary limerick usually depends on a pun or some other turn of wit. It is also likely to be somewhat suggestive or downright dirty. [Miller Williams, "Patterns of Poetry," Baton Rouge: Louisiana State University, 1986]
The place name is literally "bare ground," from Irish Liumneach, from lom "bare, thin." It was famous for hooks.

linesman.x: 1856, "private soldier in a regiment of the Line," from genitive of line (n.) + man (n.). Sports sense, in reference to umpires with specific duties in games with lines (originally tennis, also ice hockey) is from 1890.

linoleum.x: 1860, coined by English inventor Frederick Walton (1837-1928), from Latin linum "flax, linen" (see linen) + oleum "oil" (see oil (n.)) and intended to indicate "linseed-oil cloth." Originally, a preparation of solidified linseed oil used to coat canvas for making floor coverings; the word was applied to the flooring material itself after 1878. The Linoleum Manufacturing Company was formed 1864.

lipstick.x: 1880, "lip rouge molded into stick form," from lip (n.) + stick (n.). Used of lip rouge sold in pots, palettes or other shapes by 1965. Liquid lipstick is by 1938.

literati.x: "men and women of letters; the learned class as a whole," 1620s, noun use of Latin literati/litterati, plural of literatus/litteratus "educated, learned" (see literate). The proper singular would be literatus (fem. literata), though Italian literato sometimes is used in English.

lived-in.x: "inhabited, occupied" (sometimes with suggestion of "shabby, disorderly"), 1873, from verbal phrase; see live (v.) + in (adv.).

liveware.x: "people," 1966, computer-programmer jargon, from live (adj.) + ending abstracted from software, etc. Compare old nautical slang live lumber "landsmen on board a ship" (1785).

lividity.x: early 15c., "bluish or leaden color," from Old French lividite and Medieval Latin lividitatem (nominative lividitas), noun of state from past participle stem of Latin livere "be bluish" (see livid).

lobbyist.x:
1863, American English, from lobby (n.) in the political sense + -ist.
 [A] strong lobbyist will permit himself to lose heavily at the poker-table, under the assumption that the great Congressman who wins the stake will look leniently upon the little appropriation he means to ask for. [George A. Townsend, "Events at the National Capital and the Campaign of 1876," Hartford, Conn., 1876]

loblolly.x: also lob lolly, "thick gruel," especially as a typical rustic dish, also the word for a nautical medicinal remedy, 1590s, probably from lob in some sense (or perhaps it is imitative of bubbling and boiling) + lolly, an obsolete Devonshire dialect word for "broth, soup, food boiled in a pot." Compare lobscouse (1706), another obscure word for a sailor's dish. Meaning "loutish person, bumpkin" is from c. 1600. Loblolly-pine "swamp-pine, an inferior lumber-producing tree growing in the U.S. South" is from 1760.

lobotomy.x:
1936, coined from lobe (in the brain sense) + medical suffix -tomy "a cutting." Figurative use is attested from 1953. Lobectomy (attested from 1911) was in use earlier in reference to lobes of other organs (lungs, liver).
 Now I guess I'll have to tell 'em
 That I got no cerebellum
 [Ramones, "Teenage Lobotomy," 1977]

localise.x: chiefly British English spelling of localize. For suffix, see -ize. Related: Localised; localising; localisation.

localism.x: 1803, "attachment to a particular locality," from local (adj.) + -ism. Always tending toward "limitation through local attachment, provincialism." Meaning "something (especially a way of speech) characteristic of a particular locality" is from 1823.

localist.x: "one focused on local conditions," 1680s, from local (adj.) + -ist. Related: Localistic "tending to see things as of local nature or origin" (1882).

locality.x: 1620s, "fact of having a place," from French localité (16c.), from Late Latin localitatem (nominative localitas) "locality" (as a quality of bodies), from localis "belonging to a place, pertaining to a place," from Latin locus "a place, spot" (see locus). Meaning "a geographical place or district" is from 1830.

localize.x: "make local, assign to a particular place," 1792, from local (adj.) + -ize. Related: Localized; localizing; localizable (1847, originally of diseases).

locative.x: "grammatical case indicating 'place,' or 'the place wherein,'" 1804, formed as if from Latin *locativus, from locus "a place, spot, position" (see locus) on model of Latin vocativus "vocative" (from vocatus, past participle of vocare "to call, summon"). The case itself has been reconstructed as part of the Indo-European heritage and is well-preserved in some descendants, notably Sanskrit and Lithuanian; it survives elsewhere in relics, but Germanic abandoned it long ago. As an adjective by 1817, in grammatical use, 1841.

logician.x: "person skilled in logic," late 14c., from Old French logicien (13c.), from logique (see logic). The Greek word was logistes.

lollygag.x: "dawdle, dally," 1859, American English, perhaps from English dialectal lolly "tongue" + gag "deceive, trick." But see lallygag, which is attested earlier. Related: Lollygagged; lollygagging.

lonesome.x:
"drearily solitary; secluded from society; dejected from want of company," 1640s, from lone (adj.) + -some (1). Related: Lonesomeness. An older adjective was loneful (1560s).
 Loneliness expresses the uncomfortable feelings, the longing for society, of one who is alone. 
 Lonesomeness may be a lighter kind of 
 loneliness, especially a feeling less spiritual than physical, growing out of the animal instinct for society and the desire of protection, the consciousness of being alone .... 
 Lonesomeness, more often than 
 loneliness, may express the impression made upon the observer. [Century Dictionary]

long-ago.x: 1834, from the adverbial phrase, "far away in past time;" see long (adv.) + ago. As a noun from 1842.

longhand.x: also long-hand, of handwriting in full (as opposed to shorthand), 1660s, from long (adj.) + hand (n.) "handwriting."

longhorn.x: also long-horn, in reference to a type of cattle, 1808, from long (adj.) + horn (n.).

longship.x: also long-ship, Old English langscip "warship, man-of-war;" see long (adj.) + ship (n.). Translating Latin navis longa.

loophole.x: also loop-hole, mid-15c., from hole (n.). + Middle English loupe "narrow window, slit-opening in a wall" for protection of archers while shooting, or for light and ventilation (c. 1300), which, along with Medieval Latin loupa, lobia probably is a specialized word from a continental Germanic source, such as Middle Dutch lupen "to watch, peer." Figurative sense of "outlet, means of escape" is from 1660s.

lopsided.x: also lop-sided, "leaning to one side as a result of being disproportionately balanced," 1711 (lapsided), first used of ships; from lop (v.2) + side (n.). Related: Lopsidedly; lopsidedness.

lordosis.x: curvature of the spine, 1704, Modern Latin, from Greek lordosis, from lordos "bent backwards," a word of uncertain origin, with possible cognates in Armenian, Celtic, and Germanic. From 1941 in reference to the mating position assumed by some female mammals. Related: Lordotic.

lordship.x: c. 1300, from Old English hlafordscipe "authority, rule, dominion" (translating Latin dominatio); see lord (n.) + -ship. As a form of address to nobles, judges, etc., from late 15c.

loudness.x: Old English hludnis "loudness, clamor;" see loud + -ness.

love-tap.x: "gentle blow given affectionately," 1848, from love (n.) + tap (n.2).

loveless.x: early 14c., "feeling no love;" late 14c. "unloved, not attracting love," from love (n.) + -less. Attested from mid-13c. as a surname. Related: Lovelessly; lovelessness.

lovelily.x: "in a lovely way," early 14c., from lovely + -ly (2).

low-life.x: "disreputable, vulgar," 1794, from low (adj.) + life (n.). As a noun, also lowlife, "coarse, no-good person," from 1911. Low-lived (adj.) is attested from 1760.

low-rise.x: of buildings, 1957, in contrast to high-rise; see low (adv.) + rise (v.).

lucidity.x: 1650s, "brightness," from French lucidité, from Late Latin luciditas, from Latin lucidus "light, bright, clear," from lucere "to shine," from PIE *louk-eyo-, suffixed (iterative) form of root *leuk- "light, brightness." Meaning "intellectual clarity, transparency of expression" is by 1851.

luckless.x: "having no luck, suffering mischance, unsuccessful," 1560s, from luck (n.) + -less. Related: Lucklessly; lucklessness.

lug-sail.x: 1670s, probably from lug (n.) in some obscure sense; perhaps so called from the "ear" of sail formed by the oblique hang of the yard from the mast.

lustless.x: early 14c., "wanting vigor or energy," from lust (n.) + -less. From 1580s as "wanting sexual appetite."

lustrate.x: "purify by means of an offering," 1650s, from Latin lustratus, past participle of lustrare "purify ceremonially," from lustrum "purificatory sacrifice" (see lustrum) Related: Lustration (1610s).

lysosome.x: 1955, from lyso- + -some (3). So called for "their richness in hydrolytic enzymes."

Laodicean.x:
"lukewarm in religion," 1560s, from Laodicea, ancient city of Phrygia Minor (modern Latakia in Syria) whose early Christians were chastised by John the Revelator for indifference to their religion (Revelation iii:14-16).
 I knowe thy workes that thou arte nether colde ner hott: I wolde thou were colde or hotte. [Tyndale translation, 1526]
The city is said to be named for the 3c B.C.E. Syrian queen Laodice, wife of Antiochus II. Related: Laodiceanism.

Lecompton.x: in U.S. history, a reference to the town in Kansas Territory where a constitution for statehood was drawn up in 1857 by pro-slavery men.

Levantine.x: "of or pertaining to the Levant," 1640s, from Levant + -ine (1).

Levittown.x: used figuratively for "generic suburban tract housing," American English, from the vast planned real estate developments built by the firm Levitt & Sons Inc., the first on Long Island, 1946-51 (more than 17,000 homes), the second north of Philadelphia (1951-55).

Lichfield.x: city in central England, Old English Licitfelda (c. 710) "Open Land near Letocetum" (Celtic place name meaning "gray wood"), with Old English feld.

Limburger.x:
famously pungent type of cheese, 1870, short for Limburger cheese (1817), from Limburg, province in northeast Belgium, where the cheese is made. The place name is from Germanic *lindo "lime tree" (see linden) + *burg "fortification."
 Some frauds a few years ago started a Limburger cheese factory down in Keyport, New Jersey, but the imposition was soon exposed. A man could come within 300 yards of the spurious article without being knocked down, and as the smell never had any effect on the town clock the business was soon discontinued. [John E. Boyd, "The Berkeley Heroine and Others Stories," 1899]

Ljubljana.x: capital of Slovenia, the name is popularly associated with the Slavic word ljub "dear," but it is probably pre-Slavic and of obscure origin. The German form, Laibach, is from the Roman name, Labacum.

Lombardic.x: 1690s, from Lombard + -ic or from Medieval Latin Lombardicus.

Lowestoft.x: type of porcelain, named for a town in Suffolk where it was made from 1757. The place name is "Hlothver's Toft," from genitive singular of the proper name + Old Norse toft "a building lot," also "a deserted site."

Luftwaffe.x: air arm of the German Wehrmacht in the World War II era, 1935, from German Luftwaffe, literally "air-weapon," from Luft (see loft (n.)) + Waffe (see weapon (n.)).

Lusitania.x: Latin name of a region roughly corresponding to modern Portugal and part of Spain; in modern use, allusive or poetic for "Portugal." The Cunard ocean liner (sister ship of the Mauretania and Aquitania, also named after Roman Atlantic coastal provinces) was launched in 1906, torpedoed and sunk by German submarine U-20 on May 7, 1915. Related: Lusitanian.

Londoner.x: "resident or native of London," mid-15c., from London + -er (1). Earlier (late 14c.) was Londenoys, from Anglo-French Londenois.

lead-off.x: "commencement, beginning," 1879, from verbal phrase (attested from 1806); see lead (v.1) + off (adv.).

lallation.x: "imperfect pronunciation of the letter -r-, whereby it is made to sound like -l-," as typically among native speakers of Chinese and some other languages, 1864, in form a noun of action from past-participle stem of Latin lallare "sing lullaby," imitative, literally "sing 'la-la.' " See la-la and compare Greek lalein "chatter," which also is echoic. The English word was used 1640s in a sense of "childish utterance."

lamp-post.x: also lamppost, "tall pole to support a lamp or street light," by 1731, from lamp + post (n.1).

lamp-wick.x: also lampwick, "the wick of a lamp," by 1785, from lamp (n.) + wick (n.). Also name of a plant said to have been used for that purpose.

lampblack.x: also lamp-black, "pigment or ink made with pure, fine carbon, originally from the soot produced by burning oil in lamps," 1590s, see lamp (n.) + black (n.) in the sense of "a black substance" (early 15c.).

lancinate.x: "to tear, lacerate," c. 1600, from Latin lancinatus, past-participle of lancinare "tear, rend, lacerate," akin to laniare "tear," lacer "torn" (see lacerate (v.)). Related: Lancinating; lancination "sharp, shooting pain."

land-poor.x: "impoverished or in need of money while owning much unremunerative land," especially with suggestion of "poor because of land taxes and charges, by 1871, American English, identified as "a Western phrase;" see land (n.) + poor (adj.).

landloper.x: "a vagrant, one who wanders about the country, an itinerant," a 16c. variant of landleaper (late 14c., lond-lepere). Middle English Compendium considers this a native formation from land (n.) + leap (v.), perhaps influenced by or blended with Old Norse hlaup "a leap," also "a run." Compare Dutch landlooper, which also might have influenced the form, and also see interloper. Similar formation in Middle Low German lantloper, German Landläufer, Danish landlöber. Related: Landloping.

lap-dance.x:
by 1989, also a verb; see lap (n.1) + dance (n.).
 To lap dance, you undress, sit your client down, order him to stay still and fully clothed, then hover over him, making a motion that you have perfected by watching Mister Softee ice cream dispensers. [Anthony Lane, review of "Showgirls," New Yorker, Oct. 16, 1995]
In anatomy, lap is attested by late 14c. as "loose end or lobe of flesh" (as in dewlap) and from 15c.-17c. lap (often in plural) was a euphemism for "female pudendum." but this is likely not the immediate source of lap-dance.
Lap-clap was old slang for "an act of coition" (c. 1600), in warning expressions to youth often paired with lip-clip "a kiss." Also compare slang Lapland "the society of women."

lapideous.x: "stony," 1640s, from Latin lapideus, from lapid-, stem of lapis "a stone, pebble," from Proto-Italic *laped-, which de Vaan writes is "Probably a Mediterranean loanword," with cognates in Greek: lepas "bare rock, mountain," lepas "limpet," lepades "molluscs which stick to rocks."

lapidific.x: "capable of forming or converting to stone," 1690s, from French lapidifique or formed in English from Latin lapid-, stem of lapis "a stone" (see lapideous) + facere "make, do" (reconstructed to be from PIE root *dhe- "to set, put"). Related: Lapidifical (1640s); Lapidify.

largition.x: "the bestowment of a largesse, bounty," 1530s, from Old French largition and directly from Latin largitionem (nominative largitio) "a giving freely," noun of action from past-participle stem of largiri "give freely," from largus "abundant" (see large (adj.)).

latch-key.x:
also latchkey, "a key to raise or draw back the latch of a door" and allow one to enter from outside, 1775, from latch (n.) + key (n.1). Latchkey child is recorded by 1944, American English, in reference to children coming home from school while both parents are away at work.
 Many elementary school principals and teachers have always known the "latchkey" child or the "eight-hour orphan." [New York State Teachers Association, "New York State Education," 1944]
The older or simpler device was a latch-string, which could be pulled in to lock up; having it out was symbolic of openness.

latescent.x:
"tending to become latent or obscure, not obvious to perception," 1836, from Latin latescentem (nominative latescens), present participle of latescere "to hide oneself, be hidden," inchoative of latere "to lie hidden" (see latent). Related: Latescence "tendency to become obscured or lost to view."
Both words introduced in these senses by William Hamilton, professor of logic and metaphysics at the University of Edinburgh, in lectures begun in 1836 that were published in 1859, three years after his death.
 [W]hy are we not bound to suppose, that the mind may, in like manner, overlook its book of memory, and search among its magazines of latescent cognitions for the notions of which it is in want, awakening these into consciousness, and allowing the others to remain in their obscurity? [Hamilton, "Lectures on Metaphysics"]
The "Saturday Review" [June 25, 1859] praised the author generally but complained of his "wordy polemic and paraded learning," listing latescent among the words "we must submit to hear of" in the published lectures (along with orbicular, discount, explication, among others). Occasionally latescent was used from early 19c. in English botany mistakenly for lactescent.

latration.x: "barking," 1620s, noun of action from Latin latrare "to bark." Related: Latrant (adj.).

laughable.x: "fitted to excite laughter," 1590s, from laugh (v.) + -able. Related: Laughably. In this sense Old English had hleaterlic "laughterly." Laughworthy is in Ben Jonson (1610s).

laundress.x: "woman whose employment is the washing and ironing of clothes," 1540s; see laundry + -ess.

lazaretto.x: "house for reception of lepers and diseased poor persons," 1540s, from Italian lazareto "place set aside for performance of quarantine" (especially that of Venice, which received many ships from plague-infested districts in the East), from the Biblical proper name Lazarus (q.v.). Meaning "building set apart for quarantine" is c. 1600 in English. The word in Italian was perhaps influenced by the name of another hospital in Venice, that associated with the church of Santa Maria di Nazaret. Sometimes Englished as lazaret; also known as lazar house (1520s).

lazybones.x: "idler," colloquial, 1590s, from lazy + plural of bone (n.). Another form was lazyboots (1831).

leasehold.x: also lease-hold, "a tenure by lease, real estate held under a lease," 1720, from lease (n.) + hold (n.1). Related: Leaseholder.

leastways.x: 1825, obsolete colloquial, from least + way (n.). Regarded as vulgar, but simply a one-word form of Chaucer's leest weye (late 14c.). Compare leastwise (adv.) "in the least, at least," attested from 1610s, 1530s as two words.

lecherous.x: "prone to indulge in sensuality, lustful, lewd," c. 1300, probably from lecher + -ous; or else from rare Old French adjective lecheros. The nativized form is lickerish. Related: Lecherously; lecherousness.

left-wing.x: also (as an adjective) leftwing; 1530s of armies, 1882 in team sports, 1884 in politics; see left (adj.) + wing (n.).

legislate.x: "to make laws," 1805, back-formation from legislation or legislator. Related: Legislated; legislating.

lemniscus.x: "a plane curve with a characteristic 'figure-eight' shape consisting of two loops that meet at a central point," 1811, from Late Latin lemniscus "a pendent ribbon," from Greek lēmniskos "woolen ribbon, woolen tape," perhaps originally or literally "of Lemnos," the island in the Aegean, but if so the reason is obscure. Related: Lemniscate (adj.), 1781.

leukocyte.x: also leucocyte, "white blood cell, white or colorless corpuscle of the blood or lymph," 1860, via French leucocyte, from leuco-, a Latinized combining form of Greek leukos "white, clear," from PIE root *leuk- "light, brightness" + -cyte "cell."

liberally.x: late 14c., "generously, munificently," from liberal (adj.) + -ly (2). Meaning "freely" is c. 1500.

liberator.x: 1640s, from Latin liberator "one who sets free, a deliverer" (source also of French libérateur, Spanish liberador, Italian liberatore), agent noun from past participle stem of liberare "to set free" (see liberate).

libidinal.x: in psychology jargon, 1922, in Joan Riviere's translation of Freud, from combining form of libido (Latin genitive libidinis) + -al (1).

licensure.x: "a licensing, the granting of a licence," 1808, from license (v.) + -ure.

life-line.x: also lifeline, 1700, "rope used to save lives" in any way (especially for the safety of sailors on vessels in bad weather or on the yards), from life (n.) + line (n.); the figurative sense is attested by 1860. The sense in palmistry is from 1890.

life-size.x: "of the same size as the (living) original," 1820, from life (n.) + size (n.). Life-sized in the same sense is by 1811.

lifeblood.x: also life-blood, 1580s, "blood necessary for life," from life (n.) + blood (n.). Figurative and transferred use for "that which is essential to the life or strength of, that which gives vitality to" is from 1590s.

lifeguard.x: also life-guard, 1640s, "a British monarch's bodyguard of soldiers," from life (n.) + guard (n.), translating German Leibgarde. Sense of "person paid to watch over bathers" is by 1891.

lightfoot.x: "speedy, nimble," also a name for a ship or a rabbit, c. 1300 (c. 1200 as a surname) from light (adj.1) + foot (n.).

lightless.x: Old English leohtleas "dark, receiving no light;" see light (n.) + -less.

lightness.x: "quality of having little weight," late Old English lihtnesse, from light (adj.1) + -ness.

limaceous.x: "pertaining to slugs," 1650s, with -ous + Latin limax (genitive limacis) "snail, slug," from Greek leimax, from PIE root *(s)lei- "slime" (see slime (n.)). The Greek word is cognate with Russian slimák "snail," Lithuanian sliekas "earthworm," and the first element in Old English slaw-wyrm "slow-worm."

limestone.x: late 14c., from lime (n.1) + stone (n.). So called because it yields lime when burnt. Another name for it, mostly in American English, is limerock.

limpidity.x: 1650s, from French limpidité or directly from Late Latin limpiditatem (nominative limpiditas) "clarity, clearness," from Latin limpidus "clear, transparent" (see limpid). Bailey's dictionary (1727) has limpitude.

linearity.x: "state or condition of being linear," 1748, from linear + -ity.

lineation.x: late 14c., lineacioun, "a shape or contour of the body, lineament;" from late 15c. in geometry, "the act of drawing lines," from Latin lineationem (nominative lineatio) "a drawing of a line, the making in a straight line," noun of action from past-participle stem of lineare in an unrecorded sense of "trace lines" (see lineament). The meaning "a marking by lines" is attested from 1540s.

liquidity.x: 1610s, "quality of being liquid," from Late Latin liquiditatem (nominative liquiditas) "liquidity," from Latin liquidus (see liquid (adj.)). Meaning "quality of being financially liquid" is from 1897. Earlier in the literal sense was liquidness (1520s).

liquidize.x: 1837, "make liquid," from liquid (adj.) + -ize. Meaning "to run through a kitchen liquidizer" is from 1954. Related: Liquidized; liquidizing.

liquorice.x: chiefly British alternative spelling of licorice (q.v.).

lithology.x: "the study of rock-formation," a branch of geology, 1716, from Modern Latin lithologia, from litho- "rock" + -logia "study of" (see -logy). Related: Lithologic; lithologically; lithologist.

lithotomy.x: operation of cutting out a bladder stone, 1721; see litho- "stone" + -tomy "a cutting." Greek lithotomia meant "place where stone is cut; a quarry" (lithotomos is "stone-cutter").

litigator.x: 1880, "one who files lawsuits;" 1882, "one who argues lawsuits," agent noun from Latin litigare "to dispute, quarrel; go to court, litigate" (see litigation). Latin litigator meant "a party to a lawsuit; litigant;" it was translated in Old English as flitgern, flit-georn "one desirous of contention, a quarreler."

liverwort.x: late Old English liferwyrt, from lifer (see liver (n.1)) + wyrt (see wort). A loan-translation of Medieval Latin hepatica. Applied to various plants with liver-shaped leaves or that were used to treat liver disorders. Similar formation in German leberkraut.

locksmith.x: "a maker of locks," early 13c., from lock (n.1) + smith (n.).

locomotor.x: 1870, "of or pertaining to locomotion;" probably based on locomotion (as motor/motion). Earlier as a noun, "something with locomotive power" (1822). Related: Locomotory; locomotorial.

logocracy.x:
"system of government in which words are the ruling powers," 1804; see logo- + -cracy "rule or government by." Popularized by Washington Irving.
 In this country [America] every man adopts some particular slang-whanger as the standard of his judgment, and reads everything he writes, if he reads nothing else: which is doubtless the reason why the people of this 
 logocracy are so marvellously enlightened. [Irving, "Salmagundi," 1821]

logograph.x: "instrument for giving a graphic representation of speech, word-writer," 1879, from logo- "word" + -graph "instrument for recording; something written." Earliest use (1797) is in the sense "logogriph," and it frequently was used in place of that word (see logogriph). In ancient Greek, logographos was "prose-writer, chronicler, speech-writer." Related: Logographic.

logorrhea.x: 1878, from logo- "word, speech" + ending from diarrhea.

long-haul.x: 1873, originally in railroad use, in reference to the relative length of transportation, which determined the rate paid for it (long hauls = lower rate per mile); see long (adj.) + haul (n.).

long-term.x: also longterm, 1876, originally in insurance underwriting, from long (adj.) + term (n.).

love-hate.x: expressing ambivalent and strong feelings toward someone or something, 1935, originally in the jargon of psychology, from love + hate.

lowercase.x: "to set (text) in lower-case type," 1911, from lower-case (adj.). Related: Lowercased; lowercasing.

lowliness.x: early 15c., "meek or humble state of mind," from lowly + -ness. From 1590s as "humble state or condition."

luminaire.x: electric lighting unit, 1921, a trade term, from French luminaire, from Old French luminarie "lamp, candle; brightness, illumination" (see luminary).

luxuriate.x: 1620s, "grow exuberantly or in abundance," also "indulge in luxury," from Latin luxuriatus, past participle of luxuriare "have to excess," figuratively "run riot, be dissolute, indulge to excess," from luxuria "excess, rankness, luxuriance" (see luxury). Related: Luxuriated; luxuriating.

lymphatic.x: 1640s, from Modern Latin lymphaticus "pertaining to the lymph," from Latin lympha (see lymph). The English word also sometimes is used in what was the primary sense of lymphaticus in classical Latin, "mad, frenzied." OED reports this meaning "difficult to account for," but perhaps due to association of lympha with nymphe; compare Greek nymphian "to be frenzy-stricken." Also sometimes in reference to the appearance or temperament of one thought to suffer from excess of lymph, "dull, sluggish, slow in thought or action, with flabby muscles and pale skin" (1834).

Lamarckian.x: "pertaining to the theories or work of French botanist and zoologist Jean-Baptiste Pierre Antoine de Monet de Lamarck" (1744-1829). Originally (1825) in reference to his biological classification system. He had the insight, before Darwin, that all plants and animals are descended from a common primitive life-form. But in his view the process of evolution included the inheritance of characteristics acquired during life by the organism through habit, effort, or environment. The word typically refers to this aspect of his theory, which was long maintained in some quarters but has since been rejected. Related: Lamarckism, Lamarckianism.

Laurentian.x: from Latin laurentius "of or pertaining to a Lawrence" (see Laurence). In reference to granite strata in eastern Canada, attested by 1854 (Sir W.E. Logan and T. Sterry Hunt); it is named for the Laurentian Mountains (where it is found), which in turn are named for the nearby St. Lawrence River. Hence, Laurasia. The Laurentian library in Florence is named for Lorenzo (Latin Laurentius) de' Medici.

Lupercalia.x: Roman festival held Feb. 15 in honor of Lupercus a god (identified with Lycean Pan, hence regarded as a protective divinity of shepherds) who had a grotto at the foot of the Palatine Hill, from Latin Lupercalia (plural), from Lupercalis "pertaining to Lupercus," whose name derives from lupus "wolf" (see wolf (n.)). The ceremony is regarded as dating from distant antiquity. Related: Lupercalian.

lacklustre.x: also lack-lustre, chiefly British English spelling of lackluster (q.v.); for spelling, see -re.

lacustrine.x: "of or pertaining to lakes," 1825, irregularly formed from Latin lacus "lake" (see lake (n.1)). Originally in geology, of sediments. Also of animals, "living in lakes," or plants, "growing in lakes or ponds."

ladyfinger.x: also lady-finger, lady's finger, used of anything long, slender, and suggestive of grace; 1660s, originally of a type of plant; 1820 in reference to a kind of long, slender confection or sponge-cake; see lady + finger (n.).

lambdacism.x: "excessive use of the letter -l-," 1650s in writing, 1864 in pronunciation, from lambda + -ism. Also compare lallation.

lamination.x: 1670s, "action of beating into thin plates," noun of action from laminate (v.). The meaning "layer of laminated substance" is attested by 1824; that of "process of manufacturing laminated products" is attested by 1916 in advertisements for Goodyear tires, earlier as a term in metal-working (by 1851).

lamp-shade.x: also lampshade, "screen placed above or around a lighted lamp" to modify or direct the light, by 1809, from lamp + shade (n.). Earlier they were advertised simply as shades.

landocracy.x: "class which owes its political power to ownership of land," by 1836 in England, from land (n.) + -ocracy.

languorous.x: late 15c., languerous, "mournful," from Old French langoros "ill, ailing, suffering, languishing" (11c., Modern French langoureux), from langor "sickness, weakness" (see languor). The meaning "suggestive of languor, weariness, or want of energy," often with a suggestion of seductiveness, is attested by 1821. Related: Languorously; languorousness.

lapidation.x: "stoning to death," 1610s, from Latin lapidationem (nominative lapidatio) "a throwing of stones, stoning," noun of action from past-participle stem of lapidare "to throw stones at," from the stem of lapis "stone" (see lapideous).

lardaceous.x: "full of or resembling lard," 1799; see lard (n.) + -aceous.

laryngitis.x: "inflammation of the larynx," 1818, Medical Latin, from combining form of larynx (q.v.) + -itis "inflammation." Related: Laryngitic (1847).

last-ditch.x:
"on the last line of defense," 1909, from an image attested by 1715, from a quote attributed to William of Orange (1650-1702), who is said to have uttered it defiantly during the French invasion of 1672; if so, originally in a Netherlands context.
 We have no space to enter into the detail of the heroic struggle maintained by the young stadtholder and his faithful Dutchmen; how they laid their country under water, and successfully kept the powerful invader at bay. Once the contest seemed utterly hopeless. William was advised to compromise the matter, and yield up Holland as the conquest of Louis XIV. "No," replied he; "I mean to die in the last ditch." A speech alone sufficient to render his memory immortal. [Agnes Strickland, "Lives of the Queens of England," London, 1847]

laterality.x: "quality of being lateral; state or condition of having sides," 1640s; see lateral + -ity.

latibulize.x: 1802, of animals, "retire into a hiding place" (for winter), from Latin latibulare "to lie in hiding," from latibulum "a lurking place," from latere "to lurk" (see latent). In reference to persons, latibulate (v.) is attested from 1620s.

laundromat.x: "automatic coin-operated public laundry," 1946, originally (1942) a proprietary name by Westinghouse for a type of automatic washing machine; from laundry + ending probably suggested by automat. Earlier words for public clothes-washing places in U.S. were washateria (1935), laundrette (1945). Launderette is from 1947. The Westinghouse machine was popular after World War II and was available with coin chutes and timers.

laundryman.x: also laundry-man, "man employed in a laundry or engaged in the business of washing and ironing clothes," 1708; see laundry (n.) + man (n.).

lauraceous.x: "of or pertaining to the laurel family," by 1843, from Latin laurus (see laurel) + -acious.

laureation.x: 1630s, "act of crowning with laurels," originally of university students; noun of action from laureate (v.) "put a wreath of laurel upon the head of, crown with laurels," as formerly was done in conferring a degree in a university, which is from laurel (n.). Laureate (v.) is attested by 1729 as "invest with the office of poet laureate." Related: Laureated; laureating.

lawn-mower.x: 1853 as a type of machine to cut grass, from lawn (n.1) + mower. Originally pushed by hand or drawn by horses, later also powered by a motor.

lawrencium.x: 1961, Modern Latin, from the name of Ernest O. Lawrence (1901-1958), U.S. physicist, cyclotron pioneer and founder of the lab where it was discovered. With metallic element ending -ium.

legitimacy.x: "state of being legitimate" in any sense, 1690s of children, 1812 of kings and governments, general use by 1836; see legitimate (adj.) + -cy. Legitimateness (1610s) is an earlier word for it. Middle English had legitimation (mid-15c.).

lengthwise.x: "in the direction of the length," 1570s, from length + wise (n.). As an adjective by 1871.

lenticular.x: "lens-shaped, having the form of a double-convex lens," early 15c., from Late Latin lenticularis "lentil-shaped," from lenticula "a small lentil," diminutive of Latin lens "a lentil" (see lentil). Related: Lenticularity (1890).

liberalism.x: "liberal principles," especially the political principles of a liberal party, 1819, from liberal (adj.) in the political sense + -ism.

liberality.x: mid-14c., "generosity," from Old French liberalité "generosity, liberality" (13c.), from Latin liberalitatem (nominative liberalitas) "way of thinking or acting befitting a free man, frankness, affability," noun of quality from liberalis "noble, gracious; free" (see liberal (adj.)).

liberalize.x: also liberalise, "to render (more) liberal," 1774, from liberal (adj.) + -ize. Related: Liberalized; liberalizing.

life-cycle.x: "life history, whole series of vital phenomena exhibited by an organism in its development," by 1855; see life (n.) + cycle (n.).

light-year.x:
also lightyear, "distance light travels in one year" (about 5.87 trillion miles), 1888, from light (n.) + year.
A year as a measure of great distance given as time taken to cross it was in Middle English (early 14c.), 7,107 years being given as the distance from Earth to Heaven at a rate of 40 miles a day.

lightening.x: "the shedding of light," mid-14c., verbal noun from lighten (v.2). The meaning "alleviation of weight" (literal and figurative) is from 1520s, from lighten (v.1).

liquidator.x: 1825, agent noun in Latin form from liquidate (v.). By 1949 in the "killer" sense.

literalism.x: "literal interpretation or understanding," 1640s, from French littéralisme; see literal + -ism. In art, "exact rendering or representation," shading toward "unimaginative exactness."

literalist.x: "one who adheres to the exact word," 1640s, from literal + -ist. Related: Literalistic (1850).

literality.x: "quality of being literal; literal meaning," 1640s; see literal + -ity.

lithograph.x: "print made by lithography," 1828, a back-formation from lithography. As a verb, "to reproduce by lithography," from 1825. Related: Lithographed.

litholatry.x: "worship of a rock or rocks," 1868, from litho- "rock" + -latry "worship of." Related: Litholater.

locomotion.x: 1640s, "action or power of motion," from Latin loco "from a place" (ablative of locus "a place;" see locus) + motionem (nominative motio) "motion, a moving" (see motion (n.)). From 1788 as "movement from place to place."

loganberry.x: 1893, American English, named for U.S. horticulturalist James H. Logan (1841-1928), who developed it by crossing a blackberry and a raspberry.

loggerhead.x:
1580s, "stupid person, blockhead, dunce, numbskull," perhaps from dialectal logger "heavy block of wood" + head (n.). Later it meant a type of thick-headed iron tool (1680s), a type of cannon shot, a post in the stern of a whale-boat, and a type of turtle (1650s). Loggerheads "fighting, fisticuffs" is from 1670s, but the exact notion in the compound is uncertain, perhaps it suggests the heavy tool used as a weapon. The phrase at loggerheads "in disagreement" is first recorded 1670s.
 [W]e three loggerheads be: a sentence frequently written under two heads, and the reader by repeating it makes himself the third. [Grose, "Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue," 1785]

logomaniac.x: "one mad for words," 1870; see logo- "word" + maniac (see mania).

loneliness.x: 1580s, "condition of being solitary," from lonely + -ness. Meaning "feeling of being dejected from want of companionship or sympathy" is from 1814.

long-lived.x: "having long life," c. 1400, from long (adv.) + past participle of live (v.). Old English had langlife "long-lived."

longshanks.x: "long-legged person," 1550s, originally in reference to Edward I of England (1239-1307); from long (adj.) + shank (n.).

look-alike.x: "someone who closely resembles another," 1937, American English, from look (v.) + alike.

loose-leaf.x: 1899, of notebooks, ledgers, etc. made to allow insertion or removal of pages at will, from loose (adj.) + leaf (n.) "page of a book."

love-child.x: "child born out of wedlock, child of illicit love," 1798, from love (n.) + child. Compare German Liebeskind. Earlier was love brat (17c.).

loveliness.x: mid-14c., lufliness, "lovableness," from lovely + -ness. Original sense now obsolete; the meaning "exquisite beauty" is attested by c. 1600.

lovestruck.x: also love-struck, by 1762, from love (n.) + struck, from strike (v.). Love-stricken is attested from 1805.

low-budget.x: 1939, originally of motion pictures, "made with little expense;" from low (adj.) + budget (n.). Usually with a suggestion of low quality as a result.

lower-case.x: also lowercase, 1680s, in printing, "kind of type placed in the lower case," which held small letters collectively (as opposed to capitals); see lower (adj.) + case (n.2).

lumberjack.x: "one who works in a logging camp," 1831, Canadian English, from lumber (n.) + jack (n.1) "man, fellow." Lumberman in the same sense is from 1769. Timberjack "lumberman, logger" is by 1916. Timberman is attested from early 15c.

luminosity.x: 1630s, "quality of being luminous," from French luminosité (cognate with Medieval Latin luminositas "splendor") or else a native formation from luminous + -ity. Meaning "intensity of light in a color" (of a flame, spectrum, etc.) is from 1876. In astronomy, "intrinsic brightness of a heavenly body" (as distinguished from apparent magnitude, which diminishes with distance), attested from 1906.

lumpectomy.x: 1971, from lump (n.) on model of mastectomy.
